title: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own
hookLine: no power to speak or be silent, to live or die, to beg or give; the power is in His hand (Japji 33)
last: AAKHAN JOR — NO POWER TO SPEAK.

cards: Ask anyone who has taught a teenager to drive about the phantom brake. In the passenger seat, the teacher's right foot presses hard into the floor, again and again, where no pedal exists. A hand grips the door handle.
The whole body is trying to steer a car it isn't driving. It doesn't help. It just wears them out.
Plenty of people ride through life like that, gripping the outcome of the interview, the test results, the way the kids turn out.
Pauri 33 walks through almost everything a person might think they control, and taps on each one.

teach.h: NO POWER TO SPEAK, ASK, LIVE, OR DIE.
teach.b: Here's the list, in paraphrase. No power to speak, none to keep silent. None to ask, none to give.
None to live, none to die. No power to hold on to kingdoms and wealth, the things that set the mind clamoring. None over awareness, knowledge or reflection.
And one last knock on the yogis' door: no power in any technique, any jugat, to get free of the world on our own. Then the hand that holds what we don't: jis hath jor kar vekhai soe.

teach.h: THE POWER IS IN HIS HAND.
teach.b: The One in whose hand the power is, does it, and watches over it. And the final line: Nanak utam neech na koe.

teach.h: SO NO ONE IS HIGH OR LOW.
teach.b: By themselves, no one is high and no one is low. Two things to notice. First, this isn't a stanza about giving up.
A stanza ago, Japji pictured a climb step by step, and Sikh life is full of honest work and service. Sikh teachers read Pauri 33 as aimed at haumai, the ego that says I did this, all by myself.
The effort is yours to make. The power behind it isn't yours to own.
Second, where it lands. If nobody's power is their own, nobody gets to stand above anybody else. The king with his treasury and the beggar with his bowl hold exactly the same amount of jor.
It begins as letting go and ends as equality.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33 is commonly taught as a stanza against haumai, the ego that claims its own power, and its last line, no one is high or low, is often linked with Sikh teaching on equality.

o: a deep calm that comes in meditation
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
the ego that says I did it all myself

games.q: what's inside Pauri 33 — tap the pairs.
p: the One whose hand holds the power
no one is high or low

s: Pauri 33 tells people to stop trying
Sikh teachers read it as aimed at ego; honest effort and service still matter.
Pauri 33 says no technique frees us by its own power
jor na jugtee: no power in the method, one last knock on the yogis' door.
the stanza ends by saying no one is high or low

games.q: you've learned every technique for getting free of the world. what does Pauri 33 say about them?
o: the right technique will free you.
there's no power in the technique itself; the power is in His hand.
games.why: jor na jugtee chhuttai sansaar: no power in method to escape the world. jis hath jor kar vekhai soe: the One who holds the power does it, and watches.

practice: Think of one thing you're gripping right now, a result you're waiting for, a person you're worried about, a plan that might not work, and notice where the grip sits: jaw, shoulders, hands, stomach.
Open your hands, palms up, on your lap; you're not giving up on it, just taking your foot off a brake that isn't there. Breathe out, let the shoulders drop, and stay with open hands.

wordCard.voice: Haumai, the ego that says I did this alone. No power of our own to speak or be silent, to live or die, to ask or give; the power is in His hand, and so no one is high and no one is low.

carryVoice: Your line: not in my hands. The effort is yours; the power never was. Day two hundred nineteen, done.
